BREAKING: US annual interest expense is up to a record 18.5% of federal government revenue.

This is officially above the previous record of 18.4% set in 1991.

This percentage has more than QUADRUPLED over the last 4 years as interest expenditures on public debt skyrocketed.

US annual interest expense now stands at a record $1.25 trillion, more than 4x the level seen in 1991.

Meanwhile, the 30Y Treasury yield is trading at ~5.21%, just 13 basis points from its highest level since 2007.

By comparison, the 30-year yield was oscillating at ~8.00% in 1991, underscoring how much the US debt burden has grown since then.

The US debt crisis is in uncharted territory.

tweets.text:
"Until we run out of problems, we're not going to run out of demand."

Erik Torenberg, Martin Casado, Ben Horowitz, and Raghu Raghuram on why AI demand has no ceiling, and what that means for supply:

"As we've moved from chatbots to reasoning to agents to multi-agents, each step has multiplied the number of tokens a single task takes up by increasing orders of magnitude."

"The simple way to think about it is any problem that you have can be solved with enough infrastructure and money. GPUs and power, and money."

"AI's answer to getting better and better is to use more AI. Inference is one basic building block that it keeps using over and over and over again."

"In the past, money would come in, you have an engineering problem, we know that it takes two years, normally fails... [Now] there's nothing between the money going in and then the hardware creating intelligence. And so now we're just limited by our ability to create supply."

@martin_casado @bhorowitz @RaghuRaghuram @eriktorenberg

tweets.text:
US stocks are well positioned for inflation.

In 2025, the S&P 500 posted a +14.76% inflation-adjusted return, with inflation running at +2.70% for the year.

This followed real returns of +21.47% in 2024 and +22.11% in 2023.

Over the last 20 years, the largest real return was in 2013, at +30.42%, when inflation was just +1.50%.

During this period, the S&P 500 failed to beat inflation in only 4 years: 2008, 2011, 2018, and 2022.

Meanwhile, S&P 500 companies are projected to report +23% YoY earnings growth in Q3, supporting continued positive real returns even as inflation remains above 3%.

Stocks have historically been one of the best hedges against inflation.

A £29,000 Chinese SUV nicknamed the "Temu Range Rover" has outsold the actual Range Rover Evoque in its home market, the UK.

Cumulative sales of the Jaecoo 7 since January 2025 run about 58,000 against roughly 22,000 for the Evoque, more than double. It looks like a baby Range Rover and costs a fraction of one.

This is China doing to luxury autos what it did to EVs. Jaguar Land Rover leans on 3 models for about 80% of its volume, its margins are already thin, and the copycats are undercutting it at home. The badge premium that carries the whole business is being commoditized, and anyone holding legacy Western autos for the strength of the brand is watching that moat drain in real time.

China's currency is undervalued by as much as 35%, and it shows up as a discount on almost everything it makes.

Solar panels sell for about 60% less than the rest of the world charges. Heavy trucks 57% less, shoes 53%, EVs 32%. China's trade surplus is headed for $1.2 trillion this year, roughly 1% of global GDP, a level no country has reached in the postwar era.

An undervalued yuan is a subsidy stamped on every export, and it undercuts Western factories category by category. That is why Europe is furious and why officials are floating a new Plaza Accord, backed by tariffs, to force the yuan up. China is exporting deflation on an industrial scale, and stopping it takes either a revaluation or a tariff wall. Both are now on the table.

Big Pharma is walking off a $440 billion patent cliff.

The drugs that print the cash lose protection this decade. Novo Nordisk has 77% of its 2025 sales exposed by 2033, and Keytruda, a $32 billion drug, goes off patent before the decade is out. When the patents fall, generics gut the revenue within a couple of years.

The scramble to refill $440 billion of lost revenue is the bid under every takeout target in the sector. $XBI

China spent years building the world's biggest oil stockpile. A US-Iran war just showed why.

Beijing holds an estimated 1 to 1.4 billion barrels, about 120 days of imports and nearly 600 million barrels more than the US. When the war hit, it cut crude imports by 3.5 million barrels a day and leaned on reserves, so its actual demand barely moved. That is why oil never spiked on a Middle East war.

A country that imports 70% of its crude turned itself into a swing buyer that can walk away from the market for months. It caps prices now, and it is a lever Beijing can pull in a fight over Taiwan. The buffer is not infinite, though. When China flips from draining reserves to refilling them, that restocking is a bid that puts a floor back under oil.

The US just secured a majority stake in the biggest oil reserves on the planet.

Venezuela sits on about 300 billion barrels of proven crude, the largest in the world, against roughly 46 billion in the US. The deal hands Washington a 55% share on a 100-year lease, with the barrels earmarked to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Production is the gap. Venezuela pumps about 1 million barrels a day now, down from 2.4 million in 2015. Rebuilding that is more than a million barrels a day of latent supply waiting on capital and security, and Chevron is already nearing a deal to go get it. The great powers are locking up crude, and the country sitting on the most of it just opened to Western operators. $CVX

Cardboard box demand is one of the cleanest reads on the real goods economy. E-commerce was supposed to send it to the moon.

Instead, US box shipments per capita just hit a record low, below where they were in 1999. Southern pine pulpwood now fetches a 40-year low, and in some places growers are paying to have their timber hauled off rather than getting paid for it.

Amazon shrank its boxes, plastic mailers took share, and recycled and Brazilian pulp displaced domestic wood. The demand that was supposed to boom went the other way. A forest economy 6 million landowners depend on is in crisis, and the read under the e-commerce hype is simple: real goods demand is weaker than the headlines say.

tweets.text:
The last time the market churned like this was 1901.

NYSE turnover hit 319% that year, the entire market changing hands every 16 weeks, a velocity Wall Street would not match again for more than a century. Today's version is 0DTE options: more than 3 million same-day S&P 500 contracts trade every day, next to prediction markets, 100-to-1 perps, and a $1 trillion SpaceX IPO.

The 1901 fever ran hot for years before it broke. Then came the Panic of 1907 and a 30% crash, 10% of it in a single October. Velocity like this is the signature of a speculative blowoff. It can run for a while, and every prior one ended the same way, with the people holding cash buying the wreckage from the people who were sure it was different.
